english: to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')
usage: to be quick on the uptake
The whole idiom; 눈치 takes 가, never 를, with 빠르다.
to catch on / pick up on something
Here 눈치 takes 를 — it means to sense a hidden fact, e.g. 선물인 걸 눈치챘어.
Watching a person's face to gauge their reaction; can sound timid, not a compliment.
The direct opposite — missing social cues entirely.
examples: 우리 강아지는 눈치가 빨라.
Our dog is quick to read the mood.
Simplest frame: subject + 눈치가 빨라; works even for pets.
동생이 눈치가 빨라서 엄마 기분을 금방 알아채요.
My little sibling is perceptive and quickly senses Mom's mood.
Everyday: pair with 알아채다 (notice) for the 'reads + reacts' chain.
여기선 눈치가 빨라야 살아남아요.
Around here you've got to be quick on the uptake to survive.
Real office-survival nuance; 눈치가 빨라야 = 'you must be perceptive.'
nuance: 눈치 is the Korean 'social radar' for reading unspoken cues — the mood in a room, what someone really means, when to back off — and 빠르다 ('fast') frames you as catching all that quickly, so it's a warm compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. Distinguish it from 똑똑하다 ('smart/book-clever'): 똑똑하다 is raw intelligence, while 눈치가 빠르다 is interpersonal sensitivity — a person can be 똑똑하지만 눈치가 없다 (brainy yet socially oblivious). The register is casual-to-polite and common at work and among friends. Habitual partners: 분위기를 파악하다 (grasp the atmosphere), 금방 알아채다 (notice right away). The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 눈치 as eyesight because of 눈 ('eye') — it is social awareness, not vision — and using the wrong particle: it must be 눈치'가' 빠르다, whereas 'to catch on' is 눈치'를' 채다, and 'to anxiously gauge someone' is 눈치'를' 보다.

눈치가 빠르다 (perceptive, a compliment) ≠ 눈치를 보다 (nervously watching someone's reaction, often timid). They are not interchangeable and carry opposite vibes.

english: to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')
usage: The full idiom; 발 takes 이/은, and the adjective is 넓다 ('wide').
a well-connected person / a social hub
Attributive 넓은 + noun; the go-to way to describe a networker.
The opposite ('narrow feet') — knowing hardly anyone.
Near-synonym using 인맥 (人脈, 'people-vein'); slightly more formal/explicit.
examples: 우리 삼촌은 발이 넓어요.
My uncle knows a lot of people.
Plain frame: subject + 발이 넓어요.
일자리 알아보는 거면 발 넓은 선배한테 물어봐.
If you're job-hunting, ask that senior who knows everyone.
Everyday: drop 이 in casual speech (발 넓은) and tap a network.
발이 넓은 게 사회생활에선 큰 장점이에요.
Being well-connected is a big advantage in professional life.
Real-situation: nominalize with 게 to make it the subject.
nuance: Literally 'wide feet,' the image is of feet that have walked into many circles, so it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across different groups. It is a compliment about reach, and its sharper near-synonym is 인맥(人脈)이 넓다, where 인맥 ('person-vein,' a Sino-Korean word picturing connections as veins) names the network explicitly and sounds a touch more formal or business-flavored; 발이 넓다 is the warmer, more idiomatic everyday version. Register is neutral — fine in casual and polite speech alike. Natural partners: 모르는 사람이 없다 (there's nobody they don't know), 소개를 받다/시켜 주다 (get/give introductions). The key English-speaker pitfall is reading it literally (it has nothing to do with foot size) and confusing breadth with depth: 발이 넓다 means you know MANY people, not that you have many CLOSE friends — for true intimacy Koreans would say 친한 친구가 많다 instead. The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다.

english: to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')
usage: Full idiom; 손 takes 이, adjective is 크다 ('big').
Attributive 큰 + 사람; common compliment for a host.
to be stingy / always prepare too little
Opposite ('small hands') — skimping on portions or money.
Verb collocation: 크게 쓰다 = lay out money freely on others.
examples: 우리 엄마는 손이 커요.
My mom is generous (cooks a lot).
Plain frame; defaults to the cooking-amount reading.
손이 크신 분이라 선물도 늘 푸짐해요.
She's generous, so her gifts are always lavish.
Everyday: honorific 크신 + 푸짐하다 (plentiful) for gifts.
오늘 손 크게 쐈으니까 다음엔 네가 사.
I splurged today, so next time it's on you.
Real-situation: 손 크게 쏘다 (slang 쏘다 = treat) when picking up a tab.
nuance: Literally 'big hands,' the picture is of hands that scoop out a lot at once, so it praises generosity — especially cooking in big batches or spending freely to feed and host others. It carries a warm, hospitable glow rooted in Korean food culture's love of abundance (a 손 큰 host would rather over-cater than run short). Contrast it with 인심이 좋다 ('good 인심/人心, human-heartedness'), a near-synonym that stresses a kind, giving disposition in general, whereas 손이 크다 zooms in on the concrete scale of what you make or buy. Register is neutral-to-positive. Natural partners: 음식이 넘쳐나다 (food overflows), 푸짐하다 (lavish/plentiful), 회식 때 많이 사 주다 (treats a lot at company dinners). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about being a big spender on yourself or having literally large hands — it's generosity toward others; and don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = a quick, efficient worker), which is unrelated. Opposite: 손이 작다.

english: to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')
usage: Full idiom; 입 takes 이, adjective 무겁다 ('heavy').
a discreet person you can trust with secrets
Attributive 무거운 + 사람; vouches for someone's reliability.
Opposite ('light mouth') — can't keep anything quiet.
to shut one's mouth / keep quiet
Related verb; 다물다 = the concrete act of staying silent.
examples: 우리 형은 입이 무거워.
My older brother is tight-lipped.
Plain frame; states a trait.
이건 비밀인데, 너 입 무거운 거 알아서 말하는 거야.
This is a secret, but I'm telling you because I know you're discreet.
Everyday: drop 이 (입 무겁다) and use it to vouch before confiding.
변호사는 기본적으로 입이 무거워야 해요.
A lawyer fundamentally has to be tight-lipped.
Real-situation: 무거워야 하다 = professional duty of discretion.
nuance: Literally 'a heavy mouth,' the image is that words are too heavy to spill out easily, so it means you can be trusted with secrets — discreet, reliable, not a gossip. It's a compliment, typically used to reassure someone before sharing something private (말해도 돼, 걔 입 무거워). A crucial distinction: 입이 무겁다 is about confidentiality, NOT about being a quiet or shy personality in general — for that you'd say 말이 없다 ('has few words') or 과묵하다 (reserved). Register is neutral, common in both work and personal settings. Natural partners: 비밀을 지키다 (keep a secret), 신뢰를 받다 (be trusted), 믿을 수 있다 (can be relied on). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto general quietness and assuming the opposite is 입이 작다 — the true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = a leaky gossip). Keep the body-part idioms straight: heavy/light mouth = discretion, not mouth size.

english: to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')
usage: Full idiom; 귀 takes 가, adjective 얇다 ('thin').
to be on the gullible side
Softening 편이다 ('tend to be') makes self-criticism gentler.
to be won over / fall for it
Frequent partner verb: 꼬시면 바로 넘어가 = caves the moment coaxed.
examples: 나 귀가 얇아.
I'm easily swayed.
Simplest self-description with 귀가 얇다.
친구가 좋다고 하니까 귀가 얇아져서 같은 걸 샀어.
My friend said it was good, so I caved and bought the same thing.
Everyday: 귀가 얇아지다 (become swayed) in a shopping moment.
주식도 귀가 얇으면 남 말 듣고 손해 봐요.
With stocks too, if you're easily swayed you lose money following others.
Real-situation: financial warning, 남 말 듣다 = listen to others' talk.
nuance: Literally 'thin ears,' the image is ears so thin that whatever people say passes straight through and persuades you, so it describes someone easily swayed, quick to believe a recommendation, or talked into purchases. The tone is mildly negative or self-mocking, not a harsh insult (Koreans cheerfully admit 나 귀 얇아). Contrast it with 순진하다 ('naive/innocent'): 순진하다 is broad, often sympathetic innocence about the world, while 귀가 얇다 is specifically the trait of being persuaded by others' words — a 순진한 person may still hold firm, but a 귀 얇은 person flips with the last opinion they heard. Register is casual-to-polite. Natural partners: 광고 보면 자꾸 사다 (keep buying from ads), 남 말 듣고 (on others' say-so), 넘어가다 (be won over), 사기당하다 (get scammed). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about hearing ability or literally thin ears, and it must NOT be read as a compliment for being 'open-minded' or 'flexible' — it always implies a lack of one's own judgment.

Particle: it's 귀'가' 얇다 (adjective describing the ears), not 귀를 얇다.

english: to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')
usage: You are the one left waiting; often written as one word 바람맞다.
Causative 맞히다 — the subject is the no-show who ditched the other.
Totally different idiom! 피우다, not 맞다 — don't confuse the two.
a blind date (set up by someone)
The classic setting where 바람맞다 happens.
examples: 나 또 바람맞았어.
I got stood up again.
Shortest form; 바람맞다 as one word.
한 시간 기다리다가 결국 바람맞았어요.
I waited an hour and ended up getting stood up.
Everyday: 기다리다가 sets the scene before the no-show.
연락도 없이 바람맞히는 건 진짜 예의가 아니야.
Standing someone up without even a text is just rude.
Real-situation: causative 바람맞히다 to blame the no-show.
nuance: Literally 'to be hit by the wind,' the image is of someone left standing out in the wind, waiting for a person who never came — so it means getting stood up. It is most common for dates and 소개팅 (blind dates) but extends to any no-show, even a business meeting. Register is casual. The make-or-break point is the verb pairing: 바람(을) 맞다 = YOU got stood up (you are on the receiving end), while the causative 바람(을) 맞히다 = you stood SOMEONE ELSE up (you are the no-show) — swapping them reverses who is at fault. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is a near-homonym trap: 바람을 피우다 ('to raise/kindle wind') means to cheat on a romantic partner, a completely unrelated idea — saying 바람피웠어 instead of 바람맞았어 turns 'I got stood up' into 'I cheated.' Natural partners: 한 시간(이나) 기다리다 (wait a whole hour), 연락도 없이 (without even a message).

english: to lose track of time / not notice time passing (because you're absorbed/having fun)
usage: Fixed pattern; the 줄 모르다 frame = 'not realize that…'.
to not realize that (something is the case)
The grammar engine inside: verb + 는 줄 모르다.
to not even notice time passing
Natural partner adverb: 정신없이 놀다가 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
examples: 만화 보다가 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
I lost track of time reading comics.
Simple: 보다가 + the pattern; an absorbed-in-fun excuse.
오랜만에 친구 만나서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.
I met a friend after ages and totally lost track of time.
Everyday: explains a late return after catching up.
일에 집중하다 보면 시간 가는 줄 몰라요.
When I get absorbed in work, time just flies by.
Real-situation: 집중하다 보면 = 'once you get into it,' the flow state.
nuance: Literally 'to not know that time is going,' it means you were so absorbed or having such a good time that you never noticed the hours slip by — English 'time flew.' The feel is warm and positive, so it doubles as a graceful excuse for staying late or being late (게임하느라 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요). Note the contrast with 시간이 빨리 가다 ('time goes fast'): that simply observes speed, whereas 시간 가는 줄 모르다 adds the key nuance that you were unaware because you were engrossed — it's about your absorbed state, not just the clock. The load-bearing grammar is the pattern -는 줄 모르다 ('to not realize that…'), so the structure 가는 줄 모르다 must stay intact. The English-speaker pitfall: beginners drop 줄 (saying 시간 가는 모르다) and the 'didn't realize that…' meaning collapses; also avoid using it as an excuse for laziness or neglect — it implies you ENJOYED the time, not that you were careless. Natural partners: 정신없이 (absorbed), 수다 떨다가 (chatting away), 막차를 놓치다 (miss the last train).

english: to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')
usage: to sweat it out / struggle through
Full idiom; 을 is often dropped in speech (진땀 빼다).
to break out in a cold sweat
Near-synonym with 흘리다 ('shed'); heard just as often.
to break into a clammy sweat
Intransitive variant: the sweat comes out on its own.
Cousin word; 식은땀 = literally 'cooled sweat,' from a scare.
examples: 발표하다가 진땀 뺐어.
I sweated it out during the presentation.
Simple frame; casual 진땀 빼다 without 을.
면접에서 어려운 질문 받고 진땀 뺐어요.
I got a tough question in the interview and sweated it out.
Everyday: 어려운 질문을 받다 is the classic trigger; 받고 chains the cause to the struggle.
통역하느라 진땀 뺐는데 그래도 잘 끝났어요.
I had a stressful time interpreting, but it ended well.
Real-situation: -느라 names the hard task that still worked out in the end.
nuance: 진땀 is the clammy, sticky 'cold sweat' you break into under pressure — not the healthy sweat of exercise — and 빼다 ('to extract/drain') frames you as having that stress wrung out of you, so 진땀을 빼다 means to struggle through something nerve-wracking, flustered and scrambling. It captures the emotional ordeal, not mere physical exertion. Its closest near-synonym is 진땀(을) 흘리다 ('to shed cold sweat'); the meaning is essentially the same, with 빼다 leaning slightly more toward 'I got put through the wringer' and 흘리다 toward the image of sweat literally pouring. Mind the word itself: it must be 진땀 (the specific stress-sweat), not plain 땀 (ordinary sweat) — 땀을 빼다 would just mean working up a sweat or slimming down. Compare also 식은땀 ('cooled sweat'), which is the cold sweat of fear or shock specifically. Register is casual-to-polite. Natural partners: -느라 진땀 빼다 (sweat it out because of doing X), 어려운 질문을 받다 (get a tough question), 헤매다 (flounder/get lost).

english: to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic
usage: to catch one's breath / get a breather
Full idiom; 한숨 (one breath) + 돌리다 (let go round).
Different idiom! Same 한숨 but 쉬다 = the act of sighing, not relief.
to put out the most urgent fire
Natural lead-in: handle the emergency, then 한숨 돌리다.
Frequent partner adverb: 겨우 한숨 돌렸다 = only just caught my breath.
examples: 이제 좀 한숨 돌렸어.
I've finally caught my breath now.
Simple frame with 이제 ('now') marking the relief point.
시험 끝났으니까 좀 한숨 돌려.
Exams are over, so take a breather.
Everyday: imperative 돌려 telling someone to relax a bit.
급한 불은 껐으니 한숨 돌릴 수 있겠네요.
We put out the worst of it, so we can breathe now.
Real-situation: 급한 불 끄다 pairs naturally before the relief.
nuance: Literally 'to send one breath around,' it means to finally catch your breath and feel relief the moment a hectic or stressful stretch eases — the pressure has just lifted, even if only briefly. It is one of the most useful everyday relief phrases at work and home. Beware the deceptive look-alike: 한숨(을) 쉬다 uses the SAME word 한숨 but means 'to sigh' out of worry, frustration, or weariness (그는 한숨을 쉬었다 = he heaved a sigh) — a heavy, negative breath, the near-opposite feeling. The dividing line is the verb: 돌리다 (relief, you got a breather) vs 쉬다 (a worried/tired sigh). Also distinguish 쉬다 in the sense 'to rest': 한숨 돌리다 is a brief breather right after stress, not a long rest or vacation, for which you'd say 푹 쉬다 (rest fully). Register is casual-to-polite. Natural partners: 이제 (now), 겨우 (barely), 급한 불을 끄다 (put out the urgent fire), 한고비 넘기다 (get past the crisis).

english: for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')
usage: Full idiom; 김 (steam) + 새다 (leak); 김새다 is the contracted form.
for the buzz to go flat
The everyday contracted spelling you'll hear most.
Common intensifier: 김이 팍 샜어 = the mood totally deflated.
examples: 미리 결말 말하지 마, 김새잖아.
Don't spoil the ending — it ruins it.
Simple: contracted 김새다 with 잖아 ('you know it does').
기대했는데 취소돼서 김이 새 버렸어.
I was looking forward to it but it got canceled, so the excitement fizzled.
Everyday: 새 버리다 ('end up fizzling') adds finality.
같이 보려고 기다렸더니 혼자 먼저 봤다길래 김이 팍 샜어요.
I waited so we could watch it together, but they'd already watched it alone, so my excitement totally deflated.
Real-situation: 팍 (totally) intensifies; -더니/-길래 frame an anticipation spoiled by someone jumping ahead.
nuance: Literally 'the steam leaks out' — picture a hot 만두 or 김밥 going limp as its steam escapes — and it means built-up excitement or a good mood suddenly goes flat. You say it when something spoils the anticipation: a cancellation, a spoiler, a buzzkill comment, plans unraveling. Its near-synonym is 김(이) 빠지다 ('the steam drains out'), essentially interchangeable in everyday speech. Don't confuse it with 흥이 깨지다 ('the festive mood is broken') — that specifically describes a lively, party-like 흥 (merriment) being shattered, whereas 김이 새다 is the broader, quieter deflation of any built-up anticipation. Register is casual; the contracted 김새다 is the form you'll hear most, and 김 빠지다 is its twin. The English-speaker pitfall is a homonym trap: the 김 here is steam/vapor, NOT 김 the edible seaweed (laver) — there is no food in this idiom. And it describes deflated feeling, not a literal leak, so never use it for actual gas or air escaping. Natural partners: 팍 (suddenly/totally), 미리 말하다 (spoil it in advance), 반응이 없다 (no reaction).

english: to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')
usage: to be eaten up with worry
Full idiom; 속 (insides) takes 이, verb 타다 ('burn').
to fret / to make someone worry
Causative 태우다 — either you fret, or you cause others worry.
for worry to gnaw deeper and deeper
Intensified 타들어 가다 = the burning spreads inward; stronger.
Close synonym idiom with 애 (one's innards/heart): 애가 타 죽겠어.
examples: 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타.
I can't reach them and I'm worried sick.
Simple frame; 안 되다 (can't get through) triggers the worry.
합격 발표 기다리느라 속이 타요.
I'm on edge waiting for the results.
Everyday: -느라 names the anxious waiting as the cause.
부모님은 자식 일이라면 늘 속을 태우세요.
Parents always worry themselves sick over their kids.
Real-situation: causative 속을 태우다 in a habitual sense.
nuance: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry'): 걱정하다 is the everyday mental act of worrying, while 속이 타다 is the physical, churning agony of it, the way English 'worried SICK' outweighs 'worried.' A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards/heart-strings), nearly identical in force. The key grammar is the 이/을 voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the burning anxiety (it happens to you), whereas the causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone else worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다 = a child makes the parents worry). Register is casual-to-polite; intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying and who is causing the worry.

english: to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')
usage: to be jam-packed (no room to step)
Full idiom; mind the spacing: 발 디딜 (to step) + 틈이 없다.
to have not even room to step
The verb core; 디디다 = to plant your foot down.
examples: 가게가 발 디딜 틈이 없어.
The shop is jam-packed.
Simple frame; subject + 발 디딜 틈이 없어.
출근 시간 지하철은 발 디딜 틈도 없어요.
The subway at rush hour has no room to even stand.
Everyday: 틈도 없다 intensifies the rush-hour crush.
벚꽃 축제 때는 공원이 발 디딜 틈이 없어요.
During the cherry blossom festival the park is shoulder to shoulder.
Real-situation: seasonal festival crowds.
nuance: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals — anywhere overflowing with a crowd — usually with a slightly overwhelmed tone. Its Sino-Korean near-synonym is 인산인해 (人山人海, literally 'people-mountain, people-sea'), a punchier four-character idiom for an enormous throng; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational, everyday way to say it. The single most important thing to get right is spacing and the verb: it is 발 디딜 틈이 없다, where 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다, 'to set a foot down') modifies 틈 ('gap') — beginners wrongly fuse it as 발디딜. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, so don't use it for a room cluttered with objects — for that you'd say 발 디딜 곳이 없다 only loosely, or better 어질러져 있다 (it's a mess). Natural partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).
